newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech govt sets CZK 13.7 bln limit on debt buyback.
newsitem.headline: Czech govt sets CZK 13.7 bln limit on debt buyback.

text.p: The Czech government has agreed that up to 13.7 billion crowns will be used from state institutional funds to finance a scheme for buying back bad debts from small private banks, the Czech National Bank (CNB) said on Thursday.
CNB Governor Josef Tosovsky said that the money would come primarily from state-controlled Konsolidacni Banka and if necessary from the CNB itself.

Any losses from the programme would be covered by the National Property Fund (NPF), the state privatisation agency, he told a news conference. This would be in accordance with existing Czech law, he added.
Banks wanting to participate in the programme would have to fulfil conditions laid down by the CNB, he added.
Tosovsky described the measures as preventative. The maximum figure for participating banks was 100 percent of their paid-in capital plus 10 percent, he said.
The 13.7 billion crowns represented 110 percent of the total paid-in capital of small banks eligible to participate, subject to the CNB conditions.

Tosovsky's comments detailed an announcement made on Wednesday by Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus that the government had agreed to form a state company which would buy non-performing credit from the country's smaller banks.

Tosovksy said the decision followed the failure of Kreditni Banka in August. The "politicisation" of the collapse of the Plzen-based bank had undermined confidence in the banking sector overall and especially small banks, he added.
The collapse became a political hot potato between the government and opposition, and parliament has set up an inquiry into the issue.
Local media have reported a shift in deposits from small banks to the Czech Republic's "Big Four" banking institutions.

On Wednesday Klaus said the firm buying bad debts, to be called Ceska Financni sro, would be set up for a five to seven year period. The programme would be voluntary and the banks would have the option of buying the credit back later.
Kreditni Banka became the 11th small or medium-sized bank which the central bank put into forced administration or shut down in the post-Communist period.
The CNB has said the four largest banks, which comprise over 70 percent of banking activity, are basically sound and have sufficient reserves to cover their classified credit.
A central bank report to parliament in September blamed the problems of smaller banks on the lending environment surrounding the massive post-Communist privatisation programme.
